liturgical_day: Saturday of the Thirty-second Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Keep coming back to prayer
theme: Faith gives rise to prayer, and prayer steadies faith.
introduction: A widow keeps asking an unjust judge to hear her case. Jesus uses his reluctant response to teach confidence in God, whose justice and mercy are unlike the judge's indifference. Augustine connects the parable's first instruction with its final question: we need faith to pray, and we need prayer so that faith does not fail.
hero_alt: A widow appeals to a seated judge in an ancient court while Jesus teaches his disciples in a separate archway, in gold mosaic and blue stained glass.
closing: Augustine reads Jesus' final question as a summons to keep praying. Faith brings us to God; opening our hearts to him strengthens that faith. The widow's persistence gives us reason to return, with confidence in the justice and mercy of the One who hears us.
copyright_notes: Scripture is an original modernization of the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible, not of the USCCB or Vatican News Lectionary text. Every verse of Luke 18:1–8 is included. Official dated sources establish the date and Gospel citation only. Insights and expansions are original summaries of the public-domain Newman translation of the Catena Aurea, not verbatim quotations. Commentary on the immediate unit is attached to the verse it illuminates. The Douay-Rheims note on verse 3 explains 'avenge' as 'do me justice'; that sense is retained here and in the related forms in verses 5, 7, and 8.

verses.text: He also spoke a parable to them, that we ought always to pray and not lose heart.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede connects constant prayer with the appointed hours of prayer. He also counts everything a righteous person does and says toward God as prayer.
verses.commentary: Bede gives two ways to understand the command to pray always. The person who faithfully keeps the canonical hours, the appointed times of prayer, is persevering rather than giving up. This gives the command a regular place in daily life. Bede then widens the meaning: everything a righteous person does and says toward God can be counted as prayer. His brief explanation joins fidelity to set times with a life directed toward God. Prayer continues through both the hours kept and the deeds and words offered to him.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8

verses.text: He said: There was a judge in a certain city who did not fear God or regard anyone.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: The judge lacks even the restraint of shame before other people. Theophylact sees his disregard for them as a further step into wickedness.
verses.commentary: Theophylact pauses over both parts of the judge's description. Some people who do not fear God are still held back by shame before other people. That restraint does not make their condition good, but it limits how far they go. The judge has abandoned this restraint as well. He cares neither for God nor for what others think, and Theophylact says this increases the burden of his sins. The widow therefore brings her plea to someone whose character gives her no reason to expect a willing hearing.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8

verses.text: And there was a widow in that city, and she came to him, saying: Give me justice against my adversary.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine sees the widow as an image of the Church awaiting the Lord. She appears alone, though he already watches over her in secret.
verses.commentary: Augustine reads the widow as an image of the Church, which appears desolate until the Lord comes, although he already watches over her unseen. He also asks how her plea for vengeance fits with the command to pray for our enemies. The end of wickedness can come through a sinner's conversion to righteousness, or through punishment when the opportunity for conversion has passed. Even if everyone turned to God, the devil would still await condemnation. The righteous can therefore desire the final end of evil without abandoning prayer for their persecutors.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8

verses.text: For a long time he refused. But afterward he said to himself: Although I do not fear God or regard anyone,
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine says this parable teaches through contrast. The judge gives us no picture of God's character; his reluctance makes the conclusion stronger.
verses.commentary: Augustine explains that Jesus sometimes teaches by comparing similar things and sometimes by contrasting unlike things. He recalls the two debtors as an example of comparison: the one forgiven more loves more. He then recalls God's clothing of the grass as an argument that God will much more care for his people. The unjust judge belongs to this second kind of reasoning. His long refusal must be read within that contrast. The hearer is being led from the conduct of an unjust man to greater confidence in God.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8

verses.text: Yet because this widow troubles me, I will give her justice, lest she wear me out by continually coming.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: The widow gains a hearing even from an unjust judge. Augustine says those who keep praying to the source of justice and mercy have far greater reason for confidence.
verses.commentary: Augustine draws attention to what the widow's perseverance achieves. Her request is finally granted even by a judge who is thoroughly unjust. This is the lesser case from which Jesus leads his hearers to the greater one. Those who never cease praying to God should have much more confidence, because the one they approach is the source of justice and mercy. The judge's weariness explains his own decision; it does not describe God's character. His reluctant concession becomes a reason for the faithful to continue bringing their petitions to God.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8

verses.text: And the Lord said: Hear what the unjust judge says.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Jesus asks us to attend to the judge's words so that we can follow the contrast. Augustine directs our confidence toward God's justice and mercy.
verses.commentary: Augustine attaches his explanation of perseverance to Jesus' instruction to hear the judge. The judge has admitted that the widow's repeated coming will move him to act, despite his lack of concern for justice. Jesus makes that admission the starting point for confidence in God. If perseverance has prevailed with such a man, those who continue to pray to the source of justice and mercy have stronger grounds for hope. Augustine's reading keeps the reasoning of the parable in view: the unjust judge's response points beyond himself to God.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8

verses.text: And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? And will he be patient in their regard?
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: The cries of God's elect seek the final defeat of evil. Augustine explains why this hope can coexist with prayer for enemies and persecutors.
verses.commentary: Augustine links the elect's prayer with the martyrs' cry in the Book of Revelation, then holds it beside Christ's command to pray for persecutors. The two must be understood together. The righteous desire wickedness to end. A wicked person may cease to be wicked through conversion to righteousness; alternatively, punishment comes when the opportunity for conversion is lost. The devil, too, awaits final condemnation. Augustine therefore understands the elect's longing for vindication through their desire for this end, while retaining the obligation to pray for those who persecute them.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8

verses.text: I say to you that he will quickly give them justice. But when the Son of man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Faith and prayer sustain one another. Augustine says we must believe in order to pray, and pray so that our faith does not fail.
verses.commentary: Augustine understands the Lord's question as speaking of perfect faith, which is seldom found on earth. He points to the full churches as evidence that faith is present, while the promise about moving mountains exposes how far it remains from perfection. The question also brings the teaching back to prayer. When faith fails, prayer dies. We need faith in order to pray, and we must pray so that faith does not fail. Faith pours out the heart before God; that outpouring in prayer gives faith greater steadiness.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 18:1–8
